Hatchlings of the Brown goshawk emerge from calcareous eggs after an incubation period of approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] under controlled captive conditions. At the moment of hatching, the wet weight of the altricial nestling is remarkably consistent across broods, averaging 14 grams [Wwb = 14 grams]. This modest neonatal mass, typical of accipitrine raptors, marks the beginning of a rapid, food-provisioning-driven growth trajectory that is characteristic of this species. The incubating adult bird maintains this precise thermal environment through attentive brooding, ensuring optimal embryonic development. Comparisons with other members of the Accipiter genus reveal that the 30-day incubation period and 14-gram hatchling mass align closely with values reported for closely related species of similar body size, suggesting a phylogenetically conserved pattern of early ontogeny. This foundational data on birth mass and incubation length provides a crucial baseline for understanding the energetics and parental investment strategies of this Australasian raptor.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is pronounced in Accipiter fasciatus, with adult females attaining a substantially greater ultimate wet weight than their male counterparts. Field studies and measurements of breeding individuals indicate that females reach a maximum adult body mass of 580 grams [Wwi = 580 grams], whereas males achieve a considerably lighter asymptotic mass of 350 grams [Wwi = 350 grams]. This nearly two-fold difference in mass, with females being roughly 1.6 times heavier than males, is a common pattern among bird-eating accipiters and is generally interpreted as a mechanism to reduce intraspecific competition for prey resources. The larger female is capable of targeting larger avian prey items, while the smaller, more agile male specializes on smaller birds, expanding the trophic niche of the breeding pair. This size disparity also influences reproductive roles, as the larger female invests heavily in egg production and prolonged brood care, while the more maneuverable male assumes the primary role of provisioning the incubating female and the subsequent nestlings.

Data on longevity in this species, extrapolated from captive records and field observations of individual marking programs for related Accipiter species in the AnAge database, suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years] under favorable conditions at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This estimate places the Brown goshawk among the longer-lived raptors for its body size, a pace of life that is consistent with a slow life-history strategy characterized by delayed maturation and low annual reproductive output. The reproductive rate reaches a maximum of one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], with each clutch typically containing two to four eggs [N_R_i = each clutch typically containing two to four eggs]. This relatively modest annual fecundity, combined with an extended lifespan, is typical of many accipitrine hawks that invest heavily in each nesting attempt, providing extended parental care through the post-fledging dependency period. The trade-off between high survival and low fecundity underscores the species' role as a top avian predator in woodland and forest edge habitats across Australia and Papua New Guinea.

The developmental schedule of the Brown goshawk follows a tightly constrained sequence of ontogenetic milestones when measured under standard metabolic conditions at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. The fledgling achieves its first flight at 30.5 days after hatching [tx = 30.5 days after hatching], marking the transition from a stationary nestling to a mobile juvenile bird capable of short, unsteady flights at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This period is followed by a prolonged phase of somatic growth and feather maturation, during which the juvenile bird remains dependent on parental provisioning. Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation and the capacity for gametogenesis, is reached at 91.5 days after hatching [tp = 91.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively rapid progression to sexual maturity, occurring within approximately three months post-hatching, is notable for a bird that delays its first actual breeding event for several additional years. The energetic demands of achieving reproductive maturity at this early age likely require sustained high-quality foraging conditions and adequate prey availability throughout the juvenile period.

First reproduction in the Brown goshawk occurs considerably later than the attainment of physiological puberty, reflecting the social and ecological constraints typical of a territorial, long-lived raptor. The time since birth at first brood is 1095 days [tR = 1095 days], meaning that breeding individuals typically do not produce their first successful clutch until they are approximately three years old, under the thermal conditions characteristic of their active metabolic regime at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This multi-year delay between reaching sexual maturity and engaging in actual reproduction is interpreted as a period during which young birds must establish a permanent territory, acquire sufficient hunting skills to support a mate and offspring, and accumulate adequate body condition to sustain the energetic costs of egg production and incubation. Comparative analyses with other Accipiter species show that this age at first breeding is consistent with the general pattern for woodland accipiters of this body size, where delayed reproduction is favored in environments with high adult survival and saturated breeding habitat. Intraspecific variation in this timing may be linked to local prey abundance and the rate of territory turnover.
